Indemnification relations provided the earliest basis for an exception from the rule of mutuality. See First Nat. Bank v. City Nat.
Bank, 182 Mass. 130, 65 N.E. 24 (1902). The policy rationale was rooted in the substantive obligation created by the relation:
* * * [D]enial of preclusion would force an impossible choice between unacceptable alternatives. If a second action can be
maintained against the indemnitee, either the indemnitee must be allowed to assert his right of indemnification or the right must
be defeated by the judgment in favor of the indemnitor. To allow the right of indemnification would be to destroy the victory
won by the indemnitor in the first action. To deny the right of indemnification would be to destroy the indemnitee’s right by the
result of an action in which he took no part.
18A Wright, Miller & Cooper, Federal Practice and Procedure § 4463 (3d ed.).
NOTE AND QUESTIONS
How would the rule of mutuality affect the analysis in the following situations?
(a)A works for B. A, while acting within the scope of employment and driving B’s car, collides with a car driven by C. C sues A, and
judgment is for A. Subsequently B sues C for damages to the car. What effect should the earlier judgment for A have in B’s suit
against C?
(b) Suppose on the facts of (a) that C first sued B, and judgment had been for B, and C had then sued A. What effect should the earlier
judgment for B have in C’s suit against A? Would your answer be different if the second suit had been by A against C?
(c)Suppose that A, a real-estate broker, sues B, the seller of property, to recover a commission. The trial court dismisses A’s action
after trial on the ground that A had not produced C, the person who purchased the property from B and so had not established that A
was entitled to the commission. In a second action A sues C for inducing B to breach the brokerage contract causing a loss of the
commission. Can C successfully rely on the decision against A in the first action as a bar to A’s action?
(d)Suppose a mother and child are in a car accident. The mother is injured and the child dies. A, the personal representative of the
estate, brings a wrongful death action and judgment is entered for defendant. Is the mother estopped by that judgment if she later sues
to recover damages for her own injuries? Keep in mind that had the first action been successful, the mother would have been a

beneficiary of the damages award.
